messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the reply! I will check in on this - although I'll note that the file uploaded there is simply the example from the tmbstan package. In other words if you run

example(tmbstan)

on your device you'll be able to replicate the problem. Sorry if I didn't make this initially clear. This makes me think it may not be an indexing issue (I'm sure the folks who wrote the example took care of that), but maybe it is just Windows that is the problem. Thanks for your input!

Peter

On Friday, April 21, 2023 at 4:21:43 PM UTC-7 shy...@gmail.com wrote:
> Hi.
> One of the most likely possibilities might lie in an index problem.  The set of "TMB - R -  R studio" in the Windows machine is too sensitive to an error in indexing, I observe.   What I mean with an "indexing" error is a mismatch between your intending to point an element in an array and the corresponding element.   Whenever running into the mismatch problem, the R studio is forced to terminate.  This is very annoying, and thus a few friends, who use TMB, recommend we should use Linux or Mac for TMB instead of Windows.  Anyhow returning back to my main point, please check whether, in your loop (e.g., for, while, etc.) in your CPP file, your indices were correct.  Recall that the TMB index starts at zero (i.e., i =0, not i=1).   Your attachment does not show your CPP file, and thus I am not sure though that my guess is right.
> Saang-Yoon
>

> >
> > tmbstan(func)
> >
> > I get a "Fatal R Error" and am forced to restart RStudio entirely. I found this a bit odd so I wanted to make sure the simple example provided by the tmbstan package would work. I've attached a screenshot of my console output taken seconds before the fatal error (it's named Picture1.png; sorry if the quality is not fantastic but hopefully it's readable).

I'm guessing this is probably something happening in my local directory / namespace (maybe there's some function that's being over-written by another package? maybe a C++ library of some sort that I'm missing somehow?) so I've posted it here rather than as a Github issue, but if others find the same issue on their devices, maybe it's not just me.

messages.body_plain:
Peter,

Obviously, if example(tmbstan) crashes your R session there's something seriously wrong. I don't think the problem is in tmbstan though given that it works on all CRAN's 13 test systems. They all run 'example(tmbstan)' when checking the package:

https://cran.r-project.org/web/checks/check_results_tmbstan.html

On the other hand, if tmbstan is the only package causing problems you should perhaps file a bug report. Don't forget to include sessionInfo().

messages.subject: Python
messages.body_plain:
Hi.
As you know, TMB, a R package, evolved from ADMB, whose hard cores include the auto differentiation algorithm and Laplace approximation for the joint likelihood of random effects and parameters.   How can we call those hard cores in Python?  In other words, if you use the TMB or ADMB functions *in Python*, can you share the ways?
Saang-Yoon

I think this idea is worth exploring. Python has a number of ways to invoke C/C++ land Fortran libraries, but I have never tried any of them. And I have no idea of what the speed problems might be. Python is more strictly object- oriented, the Pandas package provides easier manipulation of data structures, and the graphics seem nicer to my eye. So, I hope someone gives it a try.

John

   I took a brief swing at testing it but ran into Python environment
problems that I didn't feel like troubleshooting ...

The README says

## Current

PyMB is currently just a light wrapper around Template Model Builder,
allowing users to run TMB models directly from Python by transparently
passing numpy and other numeric data into an embedded rpy2 instance. TMB
models are specified using C++ templates, requiring the user to be at
least somewhat familiar with C++.

## Future

We intend to make a fully Pythonic modeling library that closely mirrors
PyMC2 in syntax and ease of model specification, but uses either CppAD
mixed or TensorFlow under the hood.
"

messages.subject: SPDE method in TMB
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

Well, I was reviewing the implementation of the spde method here:
https://kaskr.github.io/adcomp/R__inla_8hpp_source.html
where Q is calculated as follows:
Q = kappa^4*M0 + 2*kappa^2*M0 + M1

but, in this article https://arxiv.org/pdf/1802.06350.pdf, equation 16, the mathematical expression for Q is:
Q = tau^2(kappa^4*M0 + 2*kappa^2*M0 + M1)

Probably, if you fix tau = 1, then it should not be a problem when you are doing frequentist inference, but what happens if you want to do Bayesian inference with tmbstan? "tau" in this case could has implications in the convergence of the chains.

Cheers!

messages.subject: Re: [TMB users] SPDE method in TMB
messages.body_plain:
I'm not sure that this is the best venue for discussing, but (if I remember right) kappa is the decorrelation rate per unit distance and 1/tau^2 is proportional the variance per unit distance.  The pointwise (a.k.a. marginal) variance is  then (I think) 1 / sqrt(2*pi * kappa^2 * tau^2) and the decorrelation range is sqrt(8)/kappa.  With infill asymptotics, the tau is often well-defined and asymptotically consistent while kappa is not ... hence using a kappa-variance parameterization results in neither parameter (kappa or variance) being well-behaved using infill asymptotics, which is why INLA typically uses the kappa-tau parameterization instead.  Calculating Q without tau (your first equation) is in some sense the "centered" parameterization, and it then requires scaling the random effect by 1/tau later in the model.  Calculating Q with tau (your second equation) is in some sense the "noncentered" parameterization, and it does not require transforming the random effect later.  Whether the centered or noncentered converges faster in MLE or Bayesian mixing depends on the amount of information.

messages.subject: Re: [TMB users] Fast fourier transform
messages.body_plain:
I agree with Ben that fft should be made as an atomic function. It is essentially a special case of atomic matrix multiply where the left operand is constant, so 'atomic::matmul' can be used as inspiration.
I would expect the adjoint code requires the inverse fft, so one would actually need two new atomics 'fft' and 'ifft'.
Also note that these atomics do not accept complex input/output. Manual splitting/unsplitting real- and imag parts would be needed.
Given that this is not completely straight-forward, I'm thinking it might be a useful addition to TMB. For portability reasons it's probably worth considering R's fft C-side entry point (if available).

messages.subject: Re: [TMB users] Fast fourier transform
messages.body_plain:
For what it's worth, _Numerical Recipes_ (Press et al) give an
implementation of FFT (and inverse-FFT) for real, symmetric series (so
that all imaginary parts are zero going in either direction) that
packs/unpacks the input arrays so that the algorithm doesn't
unnecessarily carry the redundant half/zero imaginary values around.

   The code should be available from the old editions of the books on
their web site; licensing doesn't allow you to directly cut and paste
the code, but if this is your actual use case it shouldn't be hard to
modify it enough to make it legal.

   I don't know if that would be better/easier than using R's
implementation and dealing with the imaginary parts.

messages.body_plain:
Mike: I think the 'Eigen::FFT'  works fine with AD. Although not complete, if I change your code to something like:

   Eigen::FFT<Type> fft;

    for (int i = 0; i < X.rows(); i++) {
      Eigen::Array<std::complex<Type>, Eigen::Dynamic, 1> fft_result(X.cols());

      Eigen::Array<Type, Eigen::Dynamic, 1> Xrow = X.row(i);
      fft.fwd(fft_result.data(), Xrow.data(), X.cols());
      //X_transformed.row(i) = fft_result.matrix();
    }

it compiles. Now you just need to fix the line that assigns complex fft_result to the real output X_transformed.

On Sunday, May 28, 2023 at 2:02:42 AM UTC+2 Ben Bolker wrote:
> For what it's worth, _Numerical Recipes_ (Press et al) give an
> implementation of FFT (and inverse-FFT) for real, symmetric series (so
> that all imaginary parts are zero going in either direction) that
> packs/unpacks the input arrays so that the algorithm doesn't
> unnecessarily carry the redundant half/zero imaginary values around.
>
> The code should be available from the old editions of the books on
> their web site; licensing doesn't allow you to directly cut and paste
> the code, but if this is your actual use case it shouldn't be hard to
> modify it enough to make it legal.
>
> I don't know if that would be better/easier than using R's
> implementation and dealing with the imaginary parts.
>
> On 2023-05-26 5:07 a.m., Kasper Kristensen wrote:
> > I agree with Ben that fft should be made as an atomic function. It is
> > essentially a special case of atomic matrix multiply where the left
> > operand is constant, so 'atomic::matmul' can be used as inspiration.
> > I would expect the adjoint code requires the inverse fft, so one would
> > actually need two new atomics 'fft' and 'ifft'.
> > Also note that these atomics do not accept complex input/output. Manual
> > splitting/unsplitting real- and imag parts would be needed.
> > Given that this is not completely straight-forward, I'm thinking it
> > might be a useful addition to TMB. For portability reasons it's probably
> > worth considering R's fft C-side entry point (if available).
> >
